setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, where people rely on what staff say and sign.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you notice moments when being straightforward is harder than going along.
detail: It is the middle of the afternoon.
pressure: {coworker3} says it is not worth the trouble.
You are in a hurry to finish.

tiers.1: Signing for something you did not verify can put people at risk.
tiers.2: A missed promise to a customer costs trust that is hard to rebuild.
tiers.3: Reporting what you saw helps the workplace keep results fair.
tiers.4: A mistake in your favor still needs to be corrected.
tiers.5: Admitting what you do not know builds more trust than guessing.

fact: {coworker} asks you to sign that a safety check was done, but you did not see it done.
issues.short: the signature for the safety check
issues.action: Decline to sign until you have seen the check done or can verify it.
issues.brief: decline to sign until it is verified
issues.reason: A signature tells others a check happened. If it did not, people could be at risk and trust in every signature drops.
issues.lesson: Sign only for what you have seen or can verify.

shortcut.text: Sign it, since {coworker} is usually reliable.
shortcut.why: A reliable person can still miss a check, and your signature would say you knew it was done.

clear: You already saw the safety check done and signed for it.
issues.done: the safety check is already verified

fact: You told a customer you would call back today, and you will not have an answer until tomorrow.
issues.action: Call today to say you do not have the answer yet and give a new time.
issues.brief: call today with an update and a new time
issues.reason: A short call keeps your word and lets the customer plan, even without the answer.
issues.lesson: Keep your promise in the way that you still can, and say honestly where things stand.

shortcut.text: Skip the call, since you have nothing to report.
shortcut.why: The customer is waiting for a call you promised, and silence suggests the promise did not matter.
shortcut.mis: A promise with no news is not a promise.

clear: You already called the customer to give an update and a new time.

fact: {coworker3} is being praised for results you know came from skipping a required step.
issues.action: Tell {lead|the} what you saw, without guessing why it happened.
issues.reason: Fair results depend on everyone following the same steps, and {lead|the} can only check what is reported.
issues.lesson: Report what you saw so results stay fair, and leave out guesses about motives.

shortcut.text: Keep quiet, since it is not your work being measured.
shortcut.brief: stay quiet because it is not your work
shortcut.why: Others who followed the steps are measured against results that were not earned the same way.
shortcut.mis: Only your own results are your concern.

clear: {Lead|the} already knows how {coworker3} reached those results.

fact: A supplier's invoice is $50 lower than the quote because of a mistake, and your team could keep the savings.
issues.short: the invoice that is $50 too low
issues.action: Tell the supplier about the error before you pay.
issues.brief: tell the supplier about the error
issues.reason: A mistake in your favor is still a mistake, and the supplier will want to know and remember that you told them.
issues.lesson: Correct mistakes that favor you as well as those that hurt you.

shortcut.text: Pay the lower amount, since the mistake was the supplier's.
shortcut.why: The amount is wrong whoever made the error, and keeping the difference is not honest.
shortcut.mis: A mistake that helps you is your good luck.

clear: The supplier already corrected the $50 invoice error.

fact: A customer asks a question you cannot fully answer, and a confident guess might sound more helpful.
issues.short: the question you cannot fully answer
issues.action: Say what you know, say what you will check, and follow up.
issues.brief: say what you know and promise to check
issues.reason: A wrong answer given with confidence costs more trust than an honest 'I will find out'.
issues.lesson: Admit what you do not know and then find out.

shortcut.text: Give your best guess confidently so they are not left waiting.
shortcut.why: A wrong guess sounds the same as a right one until it fails the customer.
shortcut.mis: Sounding sure is better than being right.

proceed.text: Carry on with your regular work, since nothing here needs action.
proceed.why: Each of these situations involves a moment when being straightforward matters.
proceed.lesson: People rely on what you say and sign, so being straightforward protects them and the trust others place in you.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} what they usually do and copy that.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the written guide, and it may be out of date.
generic.mis: Common practice is the same as the rule.

generic.text: Wait until {lead|the} brings it up before you act.
generic.why: The guide applies to you now, and waiting leaves the problem in place.
generic.mis: Someone else will raise it if it matters.

overcaution.text: Refuse to sign or promise anything at work ever again.
overcaution.why: The concern is specific. Refusing everything stops useful work and does not help anyone.
overcaution.mis: Never committing to anything is the safest way to be trusted.

setup: You find out that a report you handed in has a wrong total.

steps.text: Tell {lead|the} what was wrong and fixed
Note how you will check next time

rel: Know what is wrong before you fix it.
Understand the mistake before deciding how to prevent a repeat.
process.lesson: Check, correct, tell, then change your habit.

title: Notes on being trustworthy
intro: You are reading a coworker's draft advice on being trustworthy at work.
prompt: Which line gives advice that would harm trust?
doc.lesson: Trust is built by signing only what you verified, keeping promises and correcting mistakes, even when they favor you.

lines.text: Sign only for what you have seen or can verify.

bad.text: Sign for coworkers you trust without checking.
bad.why: A signature says you knew, and trust is not the same as knowing.

lines.text: Keep your promises, or update people before you miss one.

bad.text: If you have no news for a customer, skip the promised update.
bad.why: The customer is still waiting, and silence breaks the promise.

lines.text: Correct a mistake even when it favors you.

bad.text: Keep a benefit that came from someone else's mistake.
bad.why: The benefit is not yours, and it can damage trust if found later.

lines.text: Say when you do not know something, then find out.

review.notes: Everyday trust scenarios only. Rules are stated as what the situation requires; no law, statute or discipline is cited. Tiers: signing, promises, fair results, mistakes in your favor, honest uncertainty.
